utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll go into closed session while the witness enters the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness K90.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We'll continue with the questions. I remind you again that the solemn declaration you took to tell the truth at the beginning of your evidence continues to apply to that evidence today. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good morning again, sir. I'd like to take up where we left off yesterday, and we were talking about the crossroads, the Meja Orize-Djakovica crossroads where the check-point was. And I would like to ask you, at paragraph 54 of your statement, you say that the police seemed to be checking papers and taking money from people. I'm going to ask you that you are assuming this because you did not actually eye-witness this yourself and that's why you say it "seemed." Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yesterday, I told you that we did not really understand each other on that. The check-point at the bridge in Djakovica did exist, but this time there was the check-point at the crossroads I described to you in that diagram and that is on that little road that goes uphill, further up, towards that other part of the village. So that is where this other check-point was, the new check-point, not in Djakovica where the old check-point was, the regular check-point, but -- but, I saw them taking money.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I believe we're talking about the same check-point, the one that was near -- between your VJ command post and the rest of your unit. Is that the check-point we're talking about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the one. That's the one. Now it's that one.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, during the time-period that you were still at the VJ command post with your major, at that time you didn't personally see or eye-witness any acts of killing at the check-point. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see them kill anyone, but I did see them shoot next to people; that is to say, when they throw them to the ground and then shoot right next to them. I saw that several times because I went there several times, here and there that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And the entire time you were watching this from the VJ command post, your major was in close proximity to you, since you were his body-guard. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we were in the yard, in the same yard that is. Well, I can't explain this to you now, it's a little yard. Perhaps it's bigger than this room perhaps. It's not more than, say, ten square metres. There was this auxiliary building where the soldiers from the command platoon were and then there was high grass there, too, and then the commander didn't want to go that side. He didn't want to get wet probably. So I was there on that road, from the crossroads to the command post and in the yard. So it's that area.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So the entire time you were -- I believe you haven't answered the question entirely. I asked you while you were watching this going on from the VJ command post, was your commander, the major, with you? We're talking about the time in the command post. I don't know how we got to the tall grass in April.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tall grass in this April; there was dew in the yard. That's what I mean. We were all wet. The soldiers were wet. Now you're saying tall grass in April. I was at the command post. That's the way it was, for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And while you were at the command post, was your major with you, in close proximity to you, during the time you were at the VJ command post at all times?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, sometimes he was near me, sometimes I was a bit further away from him. Sometimes close by, sometimes further away. But when I was there, I was close to him; if I was not there, I wasn't. We talked about that for the most part. Sometimes we talked -- well, he had his own work to do and then I had my work to do, and that was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did he leave you with the impression that he had seen what you had seen at the check-point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you talked the other day about various groups of men that were allegedly separated, and you said that the earlier groups were smaller in number and that the last group was eight to ten. Now, could you please help clarify for us with respect to the sustained gun-fire that you say you heard coming from the compound, does that relate just to the last group of eight to ten persons that you said were separated and taken there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I said a few moments ago I said I think he saw it, no, I'm sure he saw what I saw, because he sent me to see what was going on with these people as they were bringing these people. And I said it was smaller groups -- well, sometimes two, three, five -- but in the last group there were ten, eight to ten. So he what I saw and I saw what -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, we have very little time, and I'm trying to finish your examination. I've asked a specific question, and I would appreciate a specific answer to my question. When you stated that you heard sustained gun-fire coming from the compound does that relate just to the last group of eight to ten individuals that you say you saw were separated and taken there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, the previous groups, too, that were taken away.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So is it your testimony that there was sustained gun-fire from the compound from 8.00 a.m. onwards until approximately what time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, from time to time. When they take people out there then the shooting would start, but in the meantime as they were being taken out, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, sir, I'd like to ask you then to comment on the fact that another witness for the Prosecution here, Mr. Pnishi at transcript pages 1470, line 18 through 1481 line 13 testified under oath that he watched this same crossroad and the same check-point from his second floor house position continuously that day until 10.30 a.m.; and, in fact, did not see or -- did not hear the sustained gun-fire and, in fact, saw men alive taken away from the school building where they had been separated.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have an objection as to foundation. I'm not sure that that question has established that we're talking about the same location. Mr. Pnishi is apparently referring to a school. I don't know that is the compound this witness is taking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the answer to the question --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Mr. Ivetic, is it? You're going to be able to make submissions about this and whether this question answered won't make any difference to the strength of these submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, could you tell me with respect to the policemen you say you saw at the compound that told you "deremo Siptare," could you tell me if this person spoke with a local Kosovar accent?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember. I don't remember. But it's not that he said that they took a knife and skinned the Siptars. He said "deremo Siptare," as in we're destroying the Siptars. Do you understand what I'm saying?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've answered the question. We don't need to go back over what you've told us several times. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, when you went to the compound and you entered it, how many bodies did you see in there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in the compound. This was an auxiliary building in the yard. I went in through the gate as if I were to walk through that door over there. The gate was on the other side and the auxiliary building was like where the Trial Chamber is sitting now. I walked into this area where there were, say, not more than three or four people lying on the floor. I didn't enter the building. I didn't go into the building, but what I saw in front of me is what I saw. I say them lying in there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: So am I correct, sir, that you looked through the gate leading into the compound and did not actually enter the building?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. I entered the yard. I entered the yard for sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Stop. Mr. Ivetic, when a witness tells you it's not a compound, then to follow that up with a question about the compound is simply inviting him to give us the same explanation yet again about why it's not a compound. Let's try and concentrate on what you really want an answer to.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour, but yesterday all day it was translated as compound to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. But you've got this explanation now that inevitably will mean -- if you want to press that, of course, that's another matter, but I think it's coincidental here to the main thrust of the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, with respect to the building, the property where the building was located, this auxiliary building, did you actually enter the yard or did you look from the area where the gate was, look through the gate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I entered the yard. I entered the yard, and on the left-hand side there was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You've answered the question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: How long were you there and were you alone.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Policemen were there. As for the military, I was there on my own. It was four or five minutes, not more than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, after you left there, did you in fact go to report this to anyone in the MUP, any MUP superiors, since yesterday you testified that there were no MUP superior officers at the location?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, but I did tell my commander. He sent me there to see what was going on over there.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: For the last handful of questions, Your Honour, I think we need to go into private session to protect the identity of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. We shall go into private session

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Witness, you have a copy of your statement -- do you have a copy of your statement in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was about to say I have a copy now of what we prepared to incorporate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, indeed, we'll come to that shortly. Will you look, please, at paragraph 60 of your statement. Now, paragraph 60 tells us what you've told us a moment ago, that your major sent you down to find out what was happening; and then you go on to say the policeman was very dismissive; and you then say that the policeman told you something. Now, just look at me now. What was it the policeman told you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He said to me: "Deremo Siptare."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I've got that. Perhaps the interpreter will now tell me the English for that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It can be interpreted in several different ways, notes the interpreter. It can indeed mean: We are destroying the Siptars. And it can literally mean skinning the Siptars as well, but it's more likely that it's just destroying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, Mr. Hannis, you have prepared another copy of the statement. Unfortunately, you haven't taken out the paragraphs that we already have said we won't be paying any attention to, so you're going to have to prepare yet another one after this.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, yes, Your Honour, and we also would prepare a redacted version of this one as well because of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I understand that. But separately from our point of view, paragraphs 2 to 23 will need to come out, since that was part of the determination we made at the outset.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honour, but I left the numbers in because I thought it was important to keep the numbering consistent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And I think you should still keep the numbering because, otherwise, the transcript won't make any sense. So even though you take out 2 to 23, this statement will go from paragraph 1 to paragraph 24 as the second paragraph. Now, you're about to give a copy of this to the witness. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I am, Your Honour. That was the first thing I wanted to do. There is one matter I want to bring to the Court's attention regarding the taking of the statement that one of the last questions --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- Mr. Ivetic asked about. I have tried to contact the individuals involved, and from the information I have so far, Your Honour, it appears there was a second interpreter who's not named on the statement. I have her name and I can provide that to the Court and Defence counsel, who was present the first day with Bretton Randall who's named on the statement, that he was involved in the portion of the statement regarding Croatia and Kosovo -- Croatia and Bosnia. I'm getting a head shake here, but let me finish and then maybe the witness will add something. And then my understanding is that John Zdrilic then completed the interview with the second interpreter who is named on the document. We haven't been able to contact Mr. Zdrilic nor reach the interpreter not mentioned on the certification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I don't know you should say any more about this, because you can obviously re-examine on the point, and it may be that that's the right way to go about this. And you may then have to decide whether the state of the evidence is so confused that you need to lead another witness later to clarify this. It may not matter, though, because what matters is what the witness says in court here and the accuracy of what is reflected in the statement, rather than the means by which it was taken. However, it's not beyond the bounds of possibility that the circumstances in which it was taken could also cast some doubt on its reliability. You have to make that assessment. Today, he has amplified the confusion by saying that perhaps the separation in time between the two dates wasn't quite as clear-cut as he said yesterday. He's also said that there was somebody who appeared on the second day that wasn't there on the first day; and, of course, the statement doesn't indicate that anyone extra arrived only for the second day. There were perhaps people there only for the first day, according to the front of the statement, but not the second. So there may be things that you wish to clarify or try to clarify, or you may decide that you'll settle for what's already there. That's a matter for you. So let's now pass over the statement. Now, how will this be numbered, Mr. Hannis? Is this P2391A perhaps?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I think this will be P02646, a completely new and different number has assigned to it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. And you want now to examine the witness about the extent to which what you've now incorporated resolves his concern about the accuracy of the statement?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour. This, as I understand it, it has been assigned that number but it's not in e-court yet, because we're trying to get the ERN numbers stamped on it and we would put it in after that process has been done. And maybe removing paragraphs 2 to 23 as you suggested, we'll do that as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, I've handed you now a copy of your statement; and if you'll be patient with my for a moment, I want to go through the changes we've made and see if they address all the concerns you had raised concerning that. Now, some of these we talked about before. The first one was paragraph 28. We changed that to read the "549th Motorised Brigade." Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And paragraph 36 regarding the use of an air-freshener can as a sort of flame-thrower, we added the words "in this situation we used," to explain that it was only on this occasion. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said "iskoristili" which means we used once. You said "koristili" which means we used continuously or more than once, but I don't object to this. Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I heard some conversation between counsel and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think this is a big difference. The witness said "iskoristili" which means we used on one just one occasion situation, on that occasion; whereas, here it says in such situations "koristili" we used. This is a form which indicates it was done regularly, not more than once; whereas, the form of the verb used by the witness would indicate it was used just in that situation on only one occasion. And I see that the witness is nodding in confirmation of this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's what I said, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What we'll do is we will alter this so that we delete the words "in this situation," and we will add the word "an" after "used," so it reads "we used an aerosol freshener can," or change "can" to the singular. And, of course, The witness has amplified that in explaining the situation in his evidence, it will be taken along with the statement. And I think that accurately reflects what can be included in the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Witness, in paragraph 39, we had omitted a reference to the man from the Territorial Defence. In your original statement, you said he worked in the territorial building -- in the municipality building. We omitted that. And in paragraph 41, we added a sentence to the first sentence to say: "It was not my unit's primary task;" and then the fourth sentence we added: "My major never ordered the expulsion of villagers; that is to say, to have them expelled to Albania."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: To Albania. It would have been better if you had said: "My major never ordered the relocation of villagers." You say "expulsion." Expulsion bears a different connotation in relation to relocation. What I said was "relocation" not "expulsion." We agreed there was no expulsion; there was only relocation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't understand your comment just now. I thought that you accepted that people were told to move in their own interests, and you described that as relocation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All that Mr. Hannis has done is make it clear that expulsion was never ordered.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. In that case, it's all right, yes. If that's how it is, then I agree. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then in paragraph 43 and 44, we changed the word "expelled" or "expulsion" to "relocation" and to "relocate."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's all right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Then in paragraph 43, we also changed "most of the villages" to "some of the villages" in the first sentence.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, that's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. And in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well -- sorry, carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In paragraph 45, where there was discussion about the looting, we have added a sentence to say: "It was not all the troops that were doing that; it was just individuals."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In paragraph 46, we added at the end of the paragraph: "What I state in this particular paragraph is not my direct knowledge but knowledge I obtained from other people."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's all right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Then in paragraph 47, we changed the next-to-the-last sentence regarding the Frenki's to now read: "They included PJP units and two or Frenki's, Frenkijevci, in a car."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said I saw two men in small hats, the kind of small hats that the units were special operations wore, and that's how it should stay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It goes on. You'll see the rest of the paragraph. It goes on: "I recognised the Frenki's men in their uniform. I swapped a cigar for some water and cigarettes. They wore the familiar Frenki's hats." Is that okay?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That's correct. And masks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that doesn't need to be added because you've given that evidence, and we have a record of it in any event.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then in paragraph 52 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just before moving from that --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- it's not clear to me that the witness was saying they were recognisable as Frenki's. He's saying they were part of a special operations unit. Now, are you saying that that special operations unit was known as Frenki's?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So why --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] PJP is the PJP; whereas, a unit for special operations or SAJ is a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, are you saying the SAJ?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] JSO.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is a JSO.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can, hopefully, clear up the confusion. I think there was an error in translation. Your question to him was translated as: Are you saying that the PJP were Frenki's men rather than the special operations unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I thought I was talking about an SAJ. Is that wrong?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: He did mention them as well yesterday, Your Honour, so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that not what is meant by a special operations unit?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It is not. The SAJ is the special anti-terrorist unit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Sorry, that's my mistake. All I want to be clear about from you, Witness K90, is what you are meaning by your reference to two Frenki's in a car. What unit did they belong to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judging by their uniforms, Your Honour, they should have been JSO; but where they came from, I don't know. We saw them on the road, on the crossroads there. We exchanged cigarettes and water, and then they went off in the direction of the village of Korenica. That was all the contact I had with those men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Why did you use the expression "two Frenki's"? Why did you call them that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Because of their hats and because of their uniforms.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Move on, please, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Paragraph 52, Witness, we -- in the first sentence, we changed the number of Albanian civilians to "around 500."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: In paragraph 55, we added in the second sentence: "They only forced the last group to sing, not all of them."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: And in 52, you also changed that part of my unit was deployed. You said "men" the first time, but now what you say is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's correct. We had changed "people" to "KLA." I'm sorry, I missed that one in paragraph 52. That was the sentence that began: "There's a small creek and they were to ensure that KLA did not escape." And then paragraph 60 --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: -- we had changed the English where it had said: "Slaughtering Siptars" to "skinning Siptars," which I now understand may be translated as "destroying Siptars." And we added a sentence: "I understood that to mean they were killing them." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you just said, I agree with that, but here you said "skinning." I didn't say -- I didn't say peeling their skin off; I just said peeling. I gave you an example. I'll give you an example. For example, you can say that Manchester skinned somebody else in football. That's what I meant.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm in your hands on how to deal with this one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, as far as the statement is concerned, we will change "skinning Siptars" to "slaughtering Siptars" and we'll take out the next part, so that we're simply expressing his understanding of what the witness said -- the policeman said rather than the exact words.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And then, Witness, in paragraph 61, we added at the end: "Only the last group had eight to ten men."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I wonder, though, if you've read carefully the previous sentence. If you look at the previous sentence where it says: "I personally saw at least four groups of men being taken to the compound and they number from five to over ten men." Now, is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wrote in my statement and I said to the Defence and I said to you when questioned by the Prosecutor that there were two, three, or four men. There weren't ten or eight every time. It was a small number. It was only the last group that there were eight to ten men, and that's what I said to the Prosecutor during the proofing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So we will delete from this "and they number from five to over ten men." We don't need to add anything. It's been explained in his oral evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I agree. So, Your Honour, should I omit the last change we made about the only the last group?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no, leave that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Witness, I didn't make any other changes. Is there something else that should be changed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you going to redact what we agreed to redact in the last statement? Names and so on?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes. The version that we propose to file publicly will be redacted as that first one was, those portions relating to names that you don't want --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In that case, I agree. Yes, that's okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Then having said that, are you satisfied and can you now attest to the Court that this statement as we modified it today is your declaration and is the evidence that you would give in this case?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, once we've prepared the changes that we made here today, then we would tender it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there -- yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, this may be more in the nature of a comment than an objection, but it seems to me that this process we've gone through with regard to this statement is similar to a long visit to a dentist. And it seems to me that where we've gotten now is that this statement as it exists now is nothing more than a -- an inartful summary of the live testimony that the witness has given in his testimony, and that it really does not provide any kind of an independent piece of evidence. And, therefore, I think maybe we've gone beyond 92 ter with the way this has all been handled and maybe the statement really serves no useful purpose at this point. But I'm not making a specific objection. I just think that 92 ter has been exceeded dramatically by the live testimony that's gone on here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are any other comments to be made by Defence counsel? The point you make, Mr. Ackerman, is a lesson I think to be learned from this. I made some comments about it yesterday. Where the evidence of a witness is to be tendered partially in writing, then there is an obligation to be careful in the preparation of that. Prior to this trial starting I spent a great deal of time in a different context trying to urge the Prosecution to prepare statements for court at an earlier stage in the pre-trial process, and, indeed, in the course of the pre-trial process in this case I made the same point. Unfortunately, for reasons that are I think matters entirely for the discretion of the Prosecution, that didn't happen. This has been a very unsatisfactory exercise in relation to this witness; however, we are sympathetic to the situation Mr. Hannis has found himself in, and we're going to take a moment to consider what exactly we should do for this statement. We are, however, quite clear in our view that in future we are unlikely to demonstrate the same patience, and it may be that the Prosecution, faced with a similar situation, will have to abandon the statement and take everything live to avoid the rather, I think, untidy exercise that's taken place here. So you should take careful note of that, Mr. Hannis, for the future. I repeat, though, we are sympathetic to the situation you found yourself in this case, and we will take that into account when deciding the motion whether to admit the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis, we will admit P2646, but it -- at the moment it's marked for identification pending the submission of its final form. And we order you to have that in our hands before the close of business today, and we allow the Defence until the end of tomorrow to make any comment about it. Now, that comment could only possibly be about something that you have changed or altered or whatever. We've had all the comments on the statement as it stands; but if there's something extraneous happens, then the Defence will have that 24 hours to comment. In the absence of comment, then it will then be admitted. But at the moment it's marked for identification. We also think it right to make clear to you at this stage that we will have particular difficulty dealing with this witness's evidence in the form of the combination of oral evidence plus the written statement because of the confusion that there has been along the way, caused by the general circumstances, including, I suppose, just the way this particular witness presents himself. That's not a criticism of him. It's his personality, possibly. We will have to evaluate that in due course, but it does underline the importance of deciding in which cases to use written statements and in which cases to present the evidence entirely viva voce. However, in recognition of what has happened in this case, all we say is that at this point we will have particular difficulty in dealing with it. So you will have to, in your submissions, have particular regard to that point and assist us from both sides to come to the right conclusion in deciding which of the statements he has made, both oral and written, we ought to accept and which we cannot accept. Now, the next stage before you continue, Mr. Hannis, is to ask counsel for the Defence whether the admission of this statement in its revised form gives rise to the need for further cross-examination. No one seeks to cross-examine; therefore, Mr. Hannis, if you have further re-examination you should continue with that now. And are we in open session?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please continue, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Before I continue I want to thank you for that because I think it would have been -- it would have -- there were particular circumstances in this situation and I appreciate your recognition of that. It would have made it very difficult if you had decided to exclude the statement because there were portions in his statement that I didn't lead evidence on if I had known the decision would be not to consider it. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, Mr. Ackerman, the first lawyer to ask you questions on the other side of the room, yesterday asked you several questions about your statement and your proofing session with the Prosecution, with me and Ms. Neema here. Your statement was delivered to your hotel room last Thursday and placed under your door; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And on last Thursday you refused to come to the office for a proofing session because you hadn't eaten or slept for a couple of days is the information I had. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't refuse. I was ill. When you ask me this, you lead me to say to the Court how it came about that I came here. Your Honours, I gave the statement as it says here in 2002. I never had any further contact with the OTP. On the 12th of September --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please, please. The question is a simple one. Whether you were unwilling to go to the office to go over the statement because you weren't up to it, having neither eaten nor slept for a couple of days. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. That's correct. I was ill. I wasn't feeling well. That's why I didn't come.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You and I probably agree that the Prosecution should have had you back earlier to take the statement and get it sorted out. You don't need to tell us that. Just concentrate on the questions that are being asked and answer them to the best of your ability. Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness K90, you didn't want to be here at all; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct. That's not correct. If I offered to give the statement, if I gave it of my own accord, my first contact with you was on the 12th of September. I was travelling, and you sent the police to subpoena me. We had had no contacts between 2002 and that point in time; then I asked you to give me time to get a passport, to prepare. You live in an orderly country. You need to prepare everything for your family in our country. You need to prepare firewood, you need to prepare food for the winter, and so on; you need to get money and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you say --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, if you had warned me in time, but you told me on the 16th of January. A friend of mine died. I attended the funeral. You said: "No problem. We will tell someone among your authorities to arrest you." And I said: "No problem." Two hours later somebody from your office called and said: "Can you come on the 23rd?" And I said, "No problem when I come back." Because on the 20th was my family's patron saint's feast. I couldn't travel then because people would come to visit my family. I don't know if you participated in that, but somebody said it would be after the 25th. Do you understand? And then it was suddenly the 23rd. First the 26th, then it was December, then it was November, then it was the 25th, and then it was the 23rd. And every time you called me you changed the date when I was supposed to testify and all under pressure and coercion. Until I met you here, not for a single moment was the conversation correct and honest. I told the lady sitting on your right the first proper contact and correct contact with the OTP was with you. Every since I began contacting the Prosecutors and the investigators. So my first proper contact, correct contact were with you and this lady.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you say "you," all those contacts with you and the OTP from September until just before you got here, you were talking not with me personally but with an investigator from the OTP; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not with you. The first time I spoke to you was when I came here, not before that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Was one character reference not good enough for you, Mr. Hannis?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Depends on the source, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, so the first time that you met me and Ms. Neema was on Friday last week when we had the proofing session?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And were you satisfied with the treatment you got during that interview? I mean, you were offered drinks and food.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, did you experience any problems in the interpretation when we were doing the proofing session? Did the young lady there seem to be doing a good job at interpreting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no problems. It was very correct. I said a few days ago my contact with you and the lady was very correct. It was the first good and correct contacts I had had with the OTP, the first one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And would it be fair to say when you first arrived on Friday and met us to start that proofing session, you were still pretty upset, excited, and agitated about everything that had happened since September in dealing with the OTP?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: All right. Now, yesterday, when Mr. Ackerman was asking you some of those questions about what you told me during the proofing session, at page 9372 being asked about the expulsion issue you said: "I can't remember everything. I can't remember exactly what we discussed." Was that -- is that a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Who talked about what? Discussed what? You? Me?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And is it fair to say -- is it fair for you to say that you can't remember everything that was discussed on Friday?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember what you and I talked about. We talked about the statement itself for not more than one hour. As for other things, we talked about it a lot more. I mean, I was there, or rather, you went about your own business and then you would come back. As for the statement, you put ten questions to me not more than that. I told you then: "No, it was not expulsion; it was relocation." [Realtime transcript read in error "No, it was expulsion, not relocation"]. And we agreed on that I think, and we agreed on other terminology, too, I think. I have my statement in the hotel, the one I brought you when I was there. On that statement, some changes were made which are now contained in the last paper you gave me. I thought that once you blackened that then that's the way it would be.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did anyone, Ms. Neema or I, ever refuse to make any of the changes you were asking for?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, an important intervention for the transcript. It's the other way around the witness said. Here it says: "We agreed that it was expulsion and not relocation." The witness said that we agreed that there was no expulsion, that it was relocation. So the transcript line is line 17.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That's helpful. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, Witness, I want to move on to some questions that Mr. Ackerman asked you beginning at page 9375, line 8. There was a long discussion about looting and that portion of your statement. And you said that there were individuals who were engaged in looting, but actually looting was a widespread problem during the conflict and it was quite common, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you have to understand. Do you think that only our army was looting and that only our army loots? People, if you have so few officers in the field, they physically simply cannot keep everything under the control. People, we did not all go there with the same intentions. There are thieves everywhere, absolutely everywhere, in any country in the world. And -- well, if you catch a thief, you send him to prison; if you don't catch him, then he'll go on stealing. There is no big philosophy about that. A thief is a thief, right? Here or there or in our country or wherever.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I wonder if you're really being fair to military people in general, Witness. I would be quick to accept your assertion about human nature, but are you suggesting that it's commonplace among regular military forces to loot?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, Your Honour, you cannot -- well, I'm not claiming that all people steal. You cannot say that the Army of Yugoslavia are thieves. I'm not a thief and these men who a sitting here are officers, they're not thieves. So it's quite illogical. There are individuals everywhere who steal. A thief is a thief; that's it. So who steals is a thief, but you cannot generally say that an entire army was looting. I was not looting. I wouldn't be the way I look now, like a church mouse. I have three children. I wouldn't look that way if I was stealing. I was in Croatia, Bosnia, Kosovo. I could have acted differently, but I mean what is there to be said about it any more than that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: One of the points I'm trying to suggest, Witness, is that for the VJ at that time, in terms of problems of criminal behaviour by soldiers, looting was one of the -- one of the biggest, if not the biggest, problem for the army. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I agree. Sir, these men who came as reservists, well, they were probably thieves even while they were civilians. Before -- I'm sure that he didn't do anything right before that if he went out there to steal. But he was summoned by the Territorial Defence, called up by the Territorial Defence. They sent him out into the territorial unit. How can the commander know who that man is until he commits a crime and then the security organs check him out and hears about it much, much later. If he was a thief there, I imagine that he was a thief while he was still a civilian. That's what I think, but that is what I think for sure. A thief is a thief. If he is used to steal, he is going to steal whenever he has an opportunity, no doubt about that. But then there were others who went to search apartments for other reasons. They were looking for what I told you about last time, drugs. There were drug addicts there. I saw this neighbour of mine there who was a drug addict and that's the only reason why he went out there. I had such a lot of trouble trying to save him. You would not believe all the things happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, in connection with this, Exhibit 962 was tendered in the Prosecution case and I think there was some reference to it in the cross-examination. This is General Delic's list of criminal reports against perpetrators in the 549th Motorised Brigade for the period from May 1998 to July 1999. And Your Honours will review that and see there are 132 separate items in there; 73 relate to theft in various forms.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, at page 9391, Mr. Ackerman asked you about the war diary entry for the 27th of April regarding the wounding of two soldiers, and Mr. Visnjic also asked you about that I think at page 9432. Now, Witness, we talked about two soldiers that were wounded on one day, and then another soldier that was -- that you knew personally. Your position is: In spite of what the war diary says about that being two incidents on two different days, your memory -- you say all three were injured on the same day. Is that correct? (redacted) I know when he was wounded. As for the two, I went with an ambulance to put them into that ambulance. To this day I claim it was on the same day. I don't know what's written there, but as far as I remember it's the same day. I already said that I don't know what date it was and then you told me that it was the 27th or the 28th; but like the other day, I'm saying that that's the way it was. So there's no change in that regard.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And are you certain that you personally were only out there at the command post and at that blockade on one day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure that I was at that blockade only one day, for sure, and not throughout the day, not the whole day at that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If the war diary indicates that some parts of the battalion were engaged in that blockade for as many as three or four days, you don't -- you personally weren't out there for that period of time. But can you say whether or not other elements of your battalion were out there for three or four days?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know about that. Possibly, but I don't know about that. I don't know anything about that for sure. I was there, on that road, where that incident occurred, the one that I testified about, only on that day, not before, not later. Sir, I went there the following day. I went there the following day. After the blockade was over, I went there the following day. I think I told you that. Remember. There wasn't any army there. There wasn't anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You were asked by Mr. Visnjic about being the squad commander. What was your rank? Did you have a rank? Were you just a private? A corporal?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a sergeant. I have my military booklet. If necessary, I'll bring it -- I'll send it, rather. That's what's written in it, too.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Finally, I, with some trepidation, would like to show the witness Exhibit P1326. This was not one that was listed on my list of exhibits to show this witness, Your Honour. It is a picture of various uniforms and it deals with the issue of the hat. We have seen this exhibit. It is in evidence. I just want to show it to the witness and ask if a hat portrayed in one of those photographs looks like the hat that he's been trying to tell us about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Witness, you'll see on your screen in a minute, I hope, a picture of -- well, a composite -- several pictures of men in uniform. I would like you to take a look at number 8 and tell us anything you can about the hat you see on the man in that picture. Do you see number 8 in the lower left-hand corner?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: In that's going to be the question, then I object to that question: Tell us anything you can about the hat.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the little hat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Hold on a second, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you enlarge it, I think that's the hat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Please pause for a moment. Thank you. What's your objection, Mr. Ivetic?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, the question that was asked was look at that picture and tell us, if you can, anything at all about the hat. I think that -- that question is improper. It calls for speculation, but, you know, he answered it shortly so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That was not a wise question in this context, Mr. Hannis. It would have been much fairer, I think, to say: Look at all these pictures and tell us if you can identify the hat anywhere. I suppose, mind you, it may be the only one with a hat that could possibly fit the bill.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No pun intended, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, you may have substantially weakened the point you're trying to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I understand the objection. I understand the point, but this is not a situation where I'm asking someone to identify the bank robber. And there's been other evidence in this case about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. We will take note of the objection, which may become a comment in due course, and we'll allow you to ask a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Have you looked at that photo and can you tell us anything about that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, the witness would like it magnified.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you have it enlarged, this picture.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How's that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's better, but I think it's pretty similar to that little hat. It's blurred, but he had a similar little hat and a similar mask. I see it a bit better now. I think it's it though it's blurred. He had a mask on his face and that kind of little hat, perhaps not this way but similar or just like that. I don't know. I mean, I think that that's the hat, since I cannot see it very well, but I think that's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K90 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am sure about the mask.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have more questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. K90, that completes your evidence -- sorry, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have an objection to some of the Prosecutor's exhibits, so I don't know whether it's a good idea to do it while the witness is still here or once he leaves the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Which exhibits?

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 1596, 1599, and 1600, photographs. It is photographs of different persons in uniform; and in view of the testimony of this witness regarding some of these photographs, perhaps it would be expedient if the Prosecutor were to give us the source of these photographs. If the Prosecutor provides us with this information, then this objection of mine perhaps may become irrelevant. I'm referring to the part of the testimony where the witness said that some of these photographs were taken in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, as -- yes, Mr. Hannis. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, my understanding is those three are already in. I think they were admitted on September 13th with Witness K73.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: But on their own, they prove nothing, Mr. Visnjic. They're only there to set context so far as this witness is concerned for the comments he's made. You're absolutely right that if the Prosecution wish to suggest that they portray people involved in the conflict in Kosovo, they have to prove that. I don't know if that's happened at an earlier stage in the context Mr. Hannis refers to, but it certainly didn't happen in the context of this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So I think you need to have no concerns about that, Mr. Visnjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VISNJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, K90, that does complete your evidence. We appreciate the difficulties that have faced you in making arrangements to come here. We thank you, nevertheless, for being here to give evidence and to assist the trial process. You're now free to leave. Thank you. We'll go into closed session for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The next witness, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next witness will be Ambassador Vollebaek, who will be led by Mr. Marcussen. I see we're about five minutes before the break. I wanted to raise with you an issue with the following witness, the protected witness. If there's a chance we're going to begin him today, I don't know when you might want to address the pending issue of protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think we should deal with it immediately before we hear the witness or at least later today and that we should make progress with the evidence of the next witness. But it may be that now's the time to take the break. I don't disagree with that. Perhaps we can review the timing. How long do you envisage being with the witness, Mr. Marcussen?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think I'm going to have more than half an hour or something like that with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Do you have any idea overall of the cross-examination, Mr. O'Sullivan?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: We haven't consulted on that, Your Honour, but I don't expect it to be very long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Well, we'll break now and we'll resume at quarter to 11.00. One other thing I should clarify for tomorrow, the sessions will be slightly differently timed tomorrow because of internal administrative arrangements. We will sit only for an hour for the first session and we will break between 10.00 and 10.30. We'll then sit from 10.30 till 12.00 and break to 12.20 probably, and sit from 12.20 to either 1.45 or 1.50, so effectively the same time but distributed differently throughout the day. We'll now adjourn until quarter to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Vollebaek.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Would you please make the solemn declaration to speak the truth by reading aloud the document which will now be placed before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We have already read a statement that you gave admittedly some time ago to the Office of the Prosecutor. We have also read the transcript of your evidence in the trial of Slobodan Milosevic. With that information before us, it's likely that examination by the Prosecution will be fairly brief. I understand that the cross-examination may not be lengthy, but it's impossible at this stage for me to tell you how long that will be. Best plan is to get started.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Very good.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the first person to examine you will be for the Prosecution, Mr. Marcussen. Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Ambassador Vollebaek, thank you for making time available to come and testify for us. I know you have a busy schedule and that it was difficult to squeeze us in. Ambassador Vollebaek, before testifying today, have you had a chance to review your statement that you gave in January 2002 to the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And when you reviewed the statement, did you note that there was an error in a date in paragraph 71 of that statement? And I'll give you a copy of the statement. I'll just open it on the right page.

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: At paragraph 71, a little under the middle, there's a reference to November 1999. Am I correct that that should have been November 1998?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: You are correct. I took over as chairman in office from the beginning of 1999, and we had this meeting in Oslo at the end of 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, apart from this correction to the statement, does the statement correctly reflect what you would declare and say if you today were examined on the points in this statement?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: It does. The English could be -- have been a little bit more elegant, but the content is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I would then seek to tender the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And its number is?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: It's number is P2634.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: 34 did you say? 4?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Yes, 4.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And, Ambassador Vollebaek, did you also have a chance to review the transcript of your testimony in the Milosevic case on the 8th of July, 2002?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And am I correct that you also discovered one error in that transcript; namely, at page 7657 at line 13, there is a problem. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, Your Honours, the transcript that I'm referring to has been uploaded into e-court, and just for reference it is P2632. And the page number that I gave before from the Milosevic transcript corresponds to page 23 of the exhibit, Exhibit P2632. Now, at line 13 of the transcript, there's a sentence that says --

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: You're talking about your meeting with Milosevic and the issue of whether or not an international force could be placed in Kosovo, and there's an issue about whether or not that is being imposed on Milosevic or not. And then you say: "And I tried to tell him that it wasn't by invitation," and that should have read: "I was trying to tell him that it was by invitation." So the idea being that Milosevic would invite OSCE or the international community to place a force in Kosovo. Is that a correct?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: That is correct, and it shows, if I remember correctly, a little bit further down in the same paragraph. But that is a misunderstanding in that statement, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think the meaning was clear, even without the correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, having cleared that up, which wasn't even necessary, the rest of the transcript, would that -- does that reflect what you would declare and say if you were examined today on these very issues?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: It does.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: So, Your Honours, I also seek the admission then of the exhibit that I mentioned, P2632.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Ambassador Vollebaek, if I could ask you to look at paragraph 19 of the statement that I handed to you before. And so we're now talking about, for the record, P2634. You say there that Mr. Sainovic was responsible for Kosovo within the federal government. What is the basis for that statement? Why are you saying he had this position?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Well, I must admit first of all that this happened eight years ago; but as I read it now and as I recall it, we were told so or I may even have read it in some kind of - what should I say? - overview of the different responsibilities of the members of the cabinet. But we were at least -- or I was at least clearly under the impression that he was the person responsible for Kosovo in the cabinet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. And there's mention in the same paragraph -- you say there was also a governor for Kosovo in Pristina. Today do you remember the name of the governor?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: His name was Zoran Andjelkovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Which is mentioned later on in the statement, just to make that clear. And then in the same paragraph, you also say that the impression at least was that decisions really were made in Belgrade. What -- what gave you that impression?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: I had, as far as I recall, three -- yes, probably three meetings in Pristina with representatives of the local government. And as far as I recall, at least at one or two times the representatives from Belgrade present in those meetings, and in addition there were never any decisions taken in the meetings. And, normally, one would refer to Belgrade or to then-President Milosevic when they said that they could not comply with what I wanted them to comply with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, in various places in your statement, you describe meetings you had with Milosevic. You explain that they were also attended by Mr. Milutinovic and sometimes by Sainovic. Could you describe the role that Mr. Milutinovic played in these meetings. Maybe the best way to do this, if you could, is to describe some of the general -- how these meetings unfolded, maybe starting with your first meeting, and just give us an impression of how these meetings worked.

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: My first meeting with President Milosevic when I -- after I became foreign minister was already in April as far as I recall 1998. But when -- in the meetings after I took over as chairman in office of the OSCE was then in January, as far as I recall the 11th of January, 1999. Normally, they would take place with a number of other people present, and I do not recall if Mr. Milutinovic would be present at all the meetings, but definitely at some of them. And he would, normally, as far as I recall anyway, sit next to Mr. Milosevic and be very supportive of Mr. Milosevic and not very supportive of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Did he address you at the meeting or --

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Normally, as far as I recall, he wouldn't. He may have made a comment or not, but maybe I was oversensitive. He had a face that spoke clearly of what he meant or thought of me and my presence and what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, at paragraph 30, if I can ask you to jump to that, that's on page 6 of the statement. In this paragraph, you describe your trip to Kosovo in March 1999. It's also covered in some other paragraphs, but we can deal with it in the context of this one. I want to ask you if you could describe what it was you saw on the ground in Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Well, we saw a lot of destruction. I do not recall all the places I visited, but as far as I recall one of the villages I visited was Podujevo, and that was a village that was quite severely damaged as far as I recall. So the houses were damaged or -- and very often the kind of -- the roofs were blown off or destroyed. So you had the kind of shells of houses without roofs. Then we met people travelling on tractors with all their belongings and whole families, and there was a lot of military presence around us, much more than should have been according to the agreement we had with Milosevic. And we also saw fires, or at least smoke then coming up from places.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And in relation to the smoke you saw coming up from the places, Milosevic told you - and you explain that in the statement - that that really was haystacks that were burning. Did you see -- were you close enough to these places that were burning to see that they were houses that were burning?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Yes, I think so. This -- again, this happened eight years ago, but there was no doubt in my mind that they were houses burning. We could see -- I don't think I was, as far as I recall, up to the houses, but we saw clusters of houses and smoke came up. And as -- when Mr. Milosevic told me on the phone that I had seen haystacks burning. Of course, I laughed because the situation wasn't laughable. But I grew up in the countryside and I know the difference between a haystack burning and a house burning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And some of the destroyed houses you saw, did they have markings that indicated that they would have been burning before you saw them?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: The houses in -- as far as I recall then, the houses in Podujevo definitely had that and I would think also some other places.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me just a minute, Your Honour. I think it would be helpful if we had a date for this visit as to whether it's within the indictment or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm about to embark on that exercise since it's not happened so far, Mr. Ackerman. I was just waiting completion of this section of the examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can I clarify with you, Mr. Vollebaek, first of all, the damage in Podujevo, can you help us with a date for that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I had -- again, Your Honour, this happened some years ago. But I had three meetings as far as I recall with Mr. Milosevic; and in connection with those meetings, I also visited Kosovo three times before the war started in 1999. As far as I recall, my first visit meeting was on the 11th of January, the second was on the 21st of January, and then I had a meeting on the 1st of March. So as far as I recall, this visit to Podujevo was in connection with this visit on the 1st of March. I would think that it must have been slightly after the 1st of March, because normally I would start a meeting in Belgrade, since that was the capital, and go to Kosovo afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And your reference to seeing smoke rising.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That was the beginning of March then, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The same visit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And the -- finally, in that section, the question of an increased military presence over that permitted by the agreement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Was at the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And can I take you back just a little further. You referred to your impression of the involvement of Mr. Milutinovic in meetings. It wasn't clear from your answer there how often you can say that you were at a meeting attended by him.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I'm -- you know, Your Honour, I was very much, I suppose, concerned with Mr. Milosevic, because he was the main actor and he was the one that addressed me, and we led the conversation. So I didn't always attach that much importance to the other people that were present. As far as I -- well, I recall him being present at meetings, but I could not honestly tell you if he was present at all the three meetings or just two of them or just one of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And your recollection is being confined to the period when you were president of the OSCE and doesn't relate to any meetings you had as foreign minister prior to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct. I do not recall whether he was present in April 1998, no. I met them --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did you only meet Milosevic on one earlier occasion prior to 1999?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I met him -- I had -- I was deputy co-chairman of the so-called International Conference to the former Yugoslavia in 1993, and I was assigned to negotiate between the government and Zagreb from June to the end of that year. And I met with him on some occasions both in Geneva, and I had a meeting with him in Belgrade at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Ambassador Vollebaek, if we turn to paragraph 39 of your statement, please, and I guess the related paragraphs would be paragraph 39, 40, and 46. The issue is about whether Mr. Milosevic and other people were told about the situation in Kosovo. Now, during the meetings you refer to here, did you -- to start with: Did you express concern about the treatment of Albanian civilians in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Yes, very much so. I think one may say more than concern. We were -- we were concerned with the situation, but we also, I guess, one could say, rejected the treatment and said that this was a breach of fundamental human rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And during these meetings, were you also giving specific examples of incidents that had taken place in Kosovo that you were aware of?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Well, I was not given examples by Mr. Milosevic, but we had examples through -- of the reports from KVM. KVM reported to us, and I would also think that there were other reports, but mainly KVM reports that told about violations of the rights that we thought meant the Kosovo Albanians should have.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And maybe my question was unclear, but that information that you got from KVM, did you relay that to -- at the meetings that were -- that you participated in?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: That is my recollection, yes. I could not give you one kind of example, but I'm fairly certain that I did so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. I just wanted to touch on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Did that question relate to whether the information was relayed to Milosevic at the meetings?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Yes. And I think the witness has explained that on occasions at least Sainovic and Milutinovic would be present at the same meetings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I'm going to have to object to the comment by my learned friend. What's been admitted into evidence - and this is my objection - is the Milosevic transcript. Now, that is the testimony -- forms part of the testimony of this witness. Now, if my learned friend is going to ask questions about what was discussed at the meeting, in my submission, he must formulate his question based on what this witness has said. In the Milosevic trial, you said this and that; is that correct? The open-ended question cannot be asked anew as if we don't have the answer given previously by this witness to discussions at these meetings, and that's what has taken place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, that's a very restrictive interpretation of what 92 ter provides. The goal-posts were moved after this trial started, and your interpretation suggests that if you use a transcript you confine yourself to the territory explored in the transcript and amplify it. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: The point I'm making on this specific bit of evidence is that if a question has been asked and answered previously, I think it's in fairness to the witness it should be put to him: This is what you said. Do you wish to add or detract from that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, that I do understand, I think, as a reasonable criticism. You'll appreciate that this is all very vague, Mr. Marcussen, especially since it's conditional on a number of things. First of all, the presence of either Messieurs Milutinovic or Sainovic at a particular meeting; secondly, that that was a meeting at which some reference was made to an atrocity reported on by the KVM. If you want to really rely on this as somehow or other giving notice to the two accused that have been mentioned by you, then I think we would need to have more precise evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honour, this has been explored and we -- I'm not able to get the evidence any clearer than it is. It would be a matter of weight and whatever's going to be made of submissions in the context of all the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, in that case - and I'm sure in the best of humour - Mr. O'Sullivan is anxious that you keep the comments to a minimum.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
