utterances.text: No, the comments -- I take the point about my -- I was trying to explain what my understanding of the evidence was. I am aware that that was my comment and not evidence, and we will be careful about that when we make submissions and not mix things up then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Ambassador Vollebaek, if I can ask you about paragraph 41. Now, here we're back to the issue that I touched upon, initially, about the international force or larger international presence in Kosovo, that you discussed with Mr. Milosevic in March 1999. Could you explain to the Court what was the proposal actually that was made for this force. How did the force look, to start?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: To explain the context a little bit, and as you know the OSCE had the political responsibility for finding a peaceful solution to the Kosovo conflict. We saw that we were not -- and -- well, to add to what I said, that we established the KVM, the observer mission, in order to be able to fulfil this task. We saw that an unarmed observer mission could not help us in fulfilling the task, and we had then the Rambouillet talks to find a solution or a way in -- by which the OSCE could continue its work. As a part of this or as a consequence of the actual situation, it was proposed that there should be an international military force. I must admit that I do not now recollect neither the composition - I don't think that we came to the stage where we discussed it - nor the actual number of personnel. But the main thing was that it should be an armed force, a military force and not an unarmed force, because that was the only way we saw that we would be able to continue. And this was very strongly then opposed by Mr. Milosevic. He would not accept an armed force on Serb territory, as he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: You made a comment at the outset of that answer, "as you know, the OSCE had the political responsibility for finding a peaceful solution to the Kosovo conflict." Now, what document provided that responsibility upon the OSCE?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, you ask a difficult question. This was -- there were different agreements between the -- between the government of Federal Republic of Yugoslavia and the OSCE that actually gave us that mandate. And that was also, as far as I can recall, agreed to by President Milosevic, and that was -- these documents were referred to in my conversations earlier then with Mr. Milosevic and the government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you're referring to an agreement that your predecessor was involved in in concluding. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Foreign Minister Geremek had an agreement, or on behalf of the OSCE, there was an agreement signed between Foreign Minister Geremek, the Polish foreign minister, and on the Yugoslav side I think it was Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And prior to that, there was an agreement that you never saw between Holbrooke and Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Marcussen, do we have exhibit numbers for these agreements?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: We do. I don't remember them on the top of my head.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We do have them?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: They are exhibits. They are 600 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Perhaps, later today, to help us to put all of this evidence in context, we should have the numbers of the relevant agreements establishing the OSCE mission, just to read them in the context of Mr. Vollebaek's evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Indeed. We'll get back to you with that in a little bit. Now, I would like if we could call up Exhibit P460, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And, Ambassador Vollebaek, that will come up on your screen in just a minute. Could we -- Ambassador Vollebaek, this is a report by the KVM from the 1st of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I'd like if we could zoom in on paragraph -- the first part of paragraph 2, the heading and that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Ambassador, can you see this on your monitor or shall we zoom in further?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: I see part of it, but -- yes. If you ask the question, I can tell you what -- now I see it finally. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, in this paragraph, there's a statement made by you about the reaction to your proposals about international military presence in Kosovo. My question simply is: Is this -- looking at this today, is that a correct reflection of what was said at the time?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Yes, I do think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: We would like to have this -- like to tender this exhibit, so that will be P460.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: In the previous trial, a bit of time was spent on the question whether the force was to be NATO-led, but this document actually clarifies that. It was to be a NATO-led force.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I guess it was to be a NATO-led force and not a UN-led force, but under a UN mandate, as you, for instance, today do have in Afghanistan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Next I would like if we could see Exhibit 461.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: While we wait for that to come up, this is the KVM report, daily report, from the subsequent days or the next day, from the 2nd of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Now, if we can zoom in on the second-last paragraph on the first page. The one that starts with: "A statement from Milutinovic's office ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Ambassador Vollebaek, can you see this? They are tweaking it a little bit.

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: If they zoom in, then it's better. Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: So this report said there was a statement from Milutinovic's office after a meeting with Ambassador Hill. And in this statement, it was said that a political agreement was not adopted at Rambouillet. Do you think that is a correct -- a correct statement?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: No, I don't think so. Could you give me the date of this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: This is the 2nd of March.

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: 2nd of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: So the day after the one we saw just now.

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: As far as I recall, I have a -- I received a letter from then-Foreign Minister Jovanovic to me with also a statement, I think, attached to it as signed by or made by Mr. Milutinovic at the time of the recess of the Rambouillet talks. As you may recall, there was talks and then a recess.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: So that's between the talks at Rambouillet and the talks at Paris?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: And after the talks in Rambouillet, the -- when there was this recess, there was, as far as I recall, an agreement or -- yes, I guess you could call it an agreement. A declaration that was signed by the Serbs but not by the Kosovo Albanians. So the problems were more actually on the Kosovo Albanian side than on the Serb side at that time, and that's why, as I see it, it is wrong to say that the Serbs had not accepted some kind of an agreement in Rambouillet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: So in your view, there was a political agreement adopted at Rambouillet, but then something changed. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: There was a political acceptance by the Serbs, and then -- but the Kosovo Albanians did not accept it; and then the leaders of the negotiations, I don't know whether they decided themselves or whether they were -- it was suggested to them that there should be a recess. And as far as I recall, it was about a two weeks' recess. And as I again recall, when the Serb delegation came back after this recess, things had changed quite dramatically, and things that they had accepted earlier all of a sudden they could not accept any longer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just hold on a moment, please, Mr. Marcussen. This is not any criticism of you, Mr. Vollebaek, but you'll understand that that answer is fairly vague. It demonstrates a change in attitude; that's as far as it goes. The reason for that is not clear, obviously, when you simply refer to things that had previously been accepted were now not accepted. There must be somebody who was neutral but so closely involved in these discussions that he can give us an accurate account of what is the state of play at the end of Rambouillet and how that may have changed when we get back to Paris, because we're hearing various accounts. We're hearing that the Albanians, for example, didn't reject agreement at Rambouillet but wanted to go back and consult before they accepted things, and that's rather from the impression you have. Who is the person -- was there not some administrator close to this keeping records who would be able to tell us what actually happened so that we could maybe have some confidence in as an unbiased observer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I hope so and I suppose so. I was not, as you also may know, a part of the negotiations as such. The chairman in office of the OSCE was an observer, so I was not present during the negotiations but I was called in when there were meetings with them. So I participated twice during this process. The negotiations were organised by the French Minister of Foreign Affairs Quai D'orsay, under the leadership of Foreign Minister Vedrine, and I suppose that the French would have taken due notes. It was also then co-chaired by the late Foreign Secretary Robin Cook, and I suppose the British would have taken due notes of this. Then you have the contact group, the five countries that were involved in this and they were around. So I certainly agree with you, Your Honour, that there should be records. I do not have them. I wasn't entitled to them at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: There will be a witness, Petric, later on who will also testify about what happened at Rambouillet. So hopefully we'll get some of this clarified at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: But -- sorry. I think that's clear. Mr. -- Ambassador Vollebaek, the last thing I wanted to ask you about concerned paragraph 74 in your statement. That is -- you describe there people leaving Kosovo. Now, I understand you were present at some point in time at the border between Kosovo and Albania.

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: That is correct. When they -- when the war started, then we withdrew the KVM observers to Macedonia, and we also then replaced some of them into Albania because there were a number of refugees, quite a large number of refugees, coming into -- both into Macedonia and to Albania. And even though the UNHCR was the main responsible UN organ -- organisation for them, we had vehicles and we had personnel that could help out. So the KVM observers were present at the borders, both in Macedonia and in Albania. And I -- at that time, as far as I recall, there was a -- quite a bit influx into Albania and there was established refugee camp just across the border in -- on the Albanian side. And I went down to meet with the people and see how they -- what was their conditions. And one of the problems we had was that they had lost identity in one way. Their ID papers were taken from them and destroyed and the licence plates on the vehicles. So we were very concerned that we should kind of re-establish or take down records of where they came from and what houses they had left and all of that. So there was a quite, as I recall it, well-organised system of doing that, and I kind of oversaw it and monitored it for a little while and then met with some of the people that came across the border and spoke to them through interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: If I can just -- when were you at the border, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: I do not recall a date. There would probably be some records in the OSCE that one could find from that visit. I had also meetings at that time with the government in Tirana. I'm afraid that I do not have a date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: But was it fairly shortly after the NATO bombing started, for example? Are we talking a few days or weeks?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: I would think not weeks, but it could of course be a week but it was shortly after. So it was at the time of the mainstream, one would say, of people fleeing Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Could you give us an impression of what you saw when you were standing at the border. Could you see into Kosovo from where you were?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: We could see into Kosovo, and I think as it's reflected in the transcript, I had never seen so many tractors in my whole life. There were thousands of them, I mean miles and miles of tractors. And people were on those hangars; whole families, couples, some people walking, but they were fairly few. Most of them were on tractors. And they had come from different areas, as far as they told me. It looked or sounded to me according to their statements very well-organised. People even talked about different ribbons or ribbons of different colours to organise their exodus.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Let -- we'll get to that a little bit. You say -- and I guess that's related. You say in your statement that a large number of people had been expelled. Now, what is it that made you say that the people had been expelled?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Well, they -- they told me that they had been expelled. There were different stories about how that expulsion had taken place. There were quite moving stories about couples or families that had been out strolling in the street in Pristina, and they came home and their apartment was occupied. Or there were other stories then of people being at home and then the police, I suppose, or someone with authority came and told them to leave. So at least those with whom I spoke were under the clear impression and, I would say, order to leave their property.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I have an objection to this line of questioning. We've had a decision in this case that with respect to certain interviews conducted with refugees and at that time it was found that without knowing the identities of the interviewees, without giving us an opportunity to confront this interview process, without having this information, it would be impossible to cross-examine on this. And now we're -- I can see we're asking where got the knowledge from is a proper question. But where the witness then proceeds to give very general but yet specific discussions of what unknown persons that we cannot compel to bring here said to him and starts making accusations against various entities that were in Kosovo-Metohija, then we're approaching an area where the Prosecution is leading evidence that I believe has already been barred in that form -- similar form in terms of the OSCE publication, As Seen, As Told. And I think we have to be mindful of the prior rulings of the Court and the inability to confront this type of evidence if it is in fact led. I think it is improper to try and lead that type of evidence particularly in light of the prior rulings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The big difference between this evidence and the evidence that was excluded is that here we have the person who is speaking directly to the people who claim to be victims. We acknowledge the point made that we don't have the identity of the people to whom he was speaking, and that obviously does affect the weight that can be given to this. But we do think that cross-examining this witness is an exercise that can assist in -- assist the Court in identifying how reliable the accounts given to the witness were. So we're in a different situation, in our opinion, from that where the evidence was rejected. We're aware of the dangers, however, of relying too heavily on hearsay of any kind, and we are aware that it must be carefully considered when it goes directly to questions of either the commission of criminal acts or the question of criminal responsibility. With these caveats in our mind, we will allow this evidence to be led.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I can, Your Honour, just one further point, though, on the objection. My -- specifically with respect to this section that was just -- that was just introduced, we don't know what the people actually said or whether he's recalling them. He said he supposes it was this; he supposes it was that. I tender that that's very vague, and it would be different if he was saying person X said A, B, C, and D. But he's giving general accounts that we can't really then to reliability because they're not tied to specific persons. They're tied to very general statements over all, and there's a lot of supposition there, et cetera. So I submit that's something that we perhaps can't really address through cross-examination because, again, we have no -- we have no supporting data. We don't have the underlying discussions that were had, the exact words that were used, the exact persons that said whatever they said. That's -- that's the difficulty I'm having with this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, the one example I think I've seen - and there may be others - but you're talking about a reference to the police, I suppose, or someone with authority. Well, I hose you know this Bench well enough by now, Mr. Ivetic, to know that if somebody says: The police, I suppose, or someone with authority, we would never come to the conclusion it was the police. What we could do eventually, of course, on an accumulation of evidence is decide it doesn't matter who precisely it was, as long as we're satisfied that they were part of a gang acting in cahoots with one another. But on the particular point, can we say that it was a policeman that was involved with any of these events? No, we couldn't so far. That may well be clarified though by other questions that are asked. I think that goes to weight. It doesn't go to the essential admissibility of the evidence. Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Ambassador Vollebaek, you started to explain something about some people getting some ribbons, and I stopped you there. Was -- could you -- now that you've given the background for this, could you explain to us what it was you were told about these ribbons. First of all, were you told what area these ribbons had been distributed, in what area of Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: What we were told --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that it was sufficient to ask what he knew about those tapes. It is leading to ask where they were distributed and who gave it to them in Kosovo. So my friend is moving a step ahead. It was sufficient to ask what the witness knew about these ribbons. All the rest is leading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, there's an element, I suppose, of leading in that question, but I don't think enough, bearing in mind the subject and the witness, to say that it would wholly undermine any answer given. We'll bear in mind the nature of the question; but, again, it's a matter that goes to weight and we will allow the question to be answered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: The witness had said that he was informed by people who exited Kosovo that they had been given ribbons. My question was based on that previous answer. It's not leading to guide the witness's attention to a specific context. And my question is, which is not leading --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, do you want us to rule against you or are you not happy with a decision in your favour?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I'm happy with a decision in my favour. I think it's important when there's an issue of weight that we get clarified if there was something wrong with my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, if you ask a question: What area were these ribbons distributed? That suggests that it's confined to an area, and that's a suggestion. Now, there's an element of leading in that. That's all we're saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Ambassador Vollebaek, were you told where these ribbons had been distributed?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: If I were told -- if I was told, I do not recollect. I was under the impression and we were told that the exodus, the expulsion, if you would call it, was well-organised. And these ribbons were mentioned to me as a sign of how well-organised it was, and it was -- I took it at that time as an indication that this was prepared. It was not something that happened -- I mean, immediately or upon some kind of immediate action. It was prepared ahead. That was how I understood it at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: What were you told about the ribbons?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: There were different colours in order for the -- whoever was along the roadside from the authority's side to guide people in the right -- on the right roads in order to avoid a traffic jam. And if you could understand that when you were standing on the border when you were looking into Kosovo, because there were, as far as I can remember, miles and miles of these tractors and it was definitely a jam on the border. And when those roads came together closer to the border, it was -- it was quite difficult for the people to came across the border. And as you will understand, they were quite eager to cross the border because they were afraid all along until they finally came over to Albania.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Marcussen, had -- Mr. Bakrac, what is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm sorry if I interrupted you while you were speaking, but I wanted to object. Would you like me to wait for you to finish and then I will object?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, objections are usually to questions. Are you objecting to an answer now?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, Your Honour. I'm objecting to the question and the answer. As for this part of the examination-in-chief, we have not received any information. This is the first time we hear about these ribbons. We will have to call back all the crime base witnesses and to cross-examine them with regard to that. Up to this moment, we had not had any information about any organisation, any ribbons, not during the 65 ter informations or in the witness statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I think some of your colleagues might be horrified at that suggestion, Mr. Bakrac. The -- I was about to ask Mr. Marcussen, if you had just given me a moment, if you were unable to find any witness at all who had a ribbon assigned to him or her as part of the exodus process. We -- this is entirely new to me. We've not heard from any refugee who had such an arrangement, although Mr. Bakrac is keen we bring them back to check.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Well -- now, the -- this witness is bringing hearsay evidence about ribbons handed out to -- having been informed that ribbons had been handed out to people who left Kosovo. That is the evidence. It's hearsay evidence. We're not stating it any higher than this. What other evidence we --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The answers that are being given are about a well-organised process to distribute streams of people crossing the border. You don't expect this Trial Chamber to make a finding to that effect about a well-organised system if you can't actually lead somebody before us that was the subject of such a system, do you?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I mean, we will have to see what all the evidence is once we are set in, and I think your comment probably means that I should clarify one thing with the witness, if I may, on this issue; namely, where --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, what about the question of notice that this is something that's never been notified to the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Obviously, the 65 ter summaries we have in this case are summaries of what the witnesses are going to say in a summary form. This witness was clearly at the border. I've asked a question about what the witness saw while at the border, and we've gotten his evidence out on this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: One -- one of the most significant issues in this case for us is linking any criminal act that's proved to have occurred to an accused or the accused. And, if I may say so, there's generally speaking not a lot of evidence that does that. So every time you come across some, it's important. And here you have a suggestion of a well-organised system to guide people out of Kosovo that might be interpreted as the essence of ethnic cleansing. And I, for one - and I can only speak for myself at this moment - would have expected that if you knew about this as the way in which the exodus was partially organised, that it might have been disclosed. Now, are you saying this is something you knew about and didn't disclose in your summary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, please. I'm speaking to Mr. Marcussen at the moment. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: I actually don't recall whether this came up in proofing. We had about a one-hour proofing session, and we did not provide --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's not in the statement. It's not in the Milosevic transcript, although that may be partly to do with the time that was wasted in the manner of cross-examination and the issues were never explored. But it certainly wasn't led by the Prosecution as part of the Milosevic case either. So where has this -- when has this emerged?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: As I said, I do not recall whether this was mentioned yesterday when we met -- when I met with Ambassador Vollebaek during proofing. I'm trying to recall. The Ambassador can probably --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, he's offering to assist and I'm happy to listen to any assistance you can give on this point, but as long as you're satisfied that what you want to say is confined to this then we'll hear you on it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I'm sorry if I have complicated things by a wrong answer, so to say. But it is correct that I don't find this in my statement. I don't know why it doesn't say this before, but we were told - and again, it is of course hearsay, because I was not witness to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I don't want you to go on to the subject matter.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What we're exploring at the moment is how it's come to the attention of a Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I mentioned it to him yesterday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It is, I'm reminded possible, that we have had some evidence that supports this from a religious leader who did - and we're speaking very much from memory at the moment and it's difficult, obviously, to recall every day everything that's been said in this case - but a religious leader who did mention carrying something white that was issued to him. So there may be some evidence. It may not be something that's never arisen. It would -- in spite whether that's right or wrong, it would be unrealistic to exclude this evidence. It's unfortunate that the pre-trial process has not involved revising the statements of witnesses and concentrating on the issues for this trial. It's very unfortunate that statements prepared for another trial are being used without revision until the last minute. We've said that before, but we think it bears repeating because it is possible that the failure to carry out that simple exercise may prejudice this -- the outcome of this trial adversely for the Prosecution. Nevertheless, we will allow this evidence to be led. If it gives rise to difficulty for the Defence, then we will have to address that difficulty and accord them any necessary remedy to ensure that there's no unfairness attributable to the admission of this evidence. Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I think I would actually stop with the witness at that point in time and stop the direct examination for now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Your period, Mr. Vollebaek, at the border when you had an opportunity to speak to people was confined to one day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Over roughly what period of time in that day did you speak to people directly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We -- as far as I recall, we came up from Tirana and so I think it would have been midday or -- before noon or noontime or something like that, and then we stayed until the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Were you involved in individual discussions with people or were you observing the process that your staff were engaged in, in finding out details from refugees arriving?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was observing, Your Honour. I was getting up to the border and seeing the -- watching the various activities going on because there were a number of organisations involved in this. People had travelled for some time, so there was an organisation giving them a bottle of water as soon as they crossed and then a loaf of bread the next stop; and then the third stop, as far as I recall, was the OSCE or the KVM then taking down their data. So I was standing close to the border, and through interpreters I spoke to people as they crossed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: So you yourself posed questions to these people or exchanged conversation with them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Through an interpreter, yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And did you also listen to what was being said between your own staff interviewing them and recording their details and the refugees themselves?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, for a short while, but not for a long time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Okay. Mr. O'Sullivan, the order?

utterances.speaker: MR. O'SULLIVAN
utterances.text: I will follow the indictment and I have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I do have questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Vollebaek, good day. My name is Toma Fila, attorney-at-law, appearing for Nikola Sainovic. I would like to begin with the issue of Rambouillet and what you said about it. MR. FILA [Interpretation] I wish to remind the Chamber that Mr. O'Sullivan tendered as a Defence exhibit a book of documents from Rambouillet. The Chamber has these, and it contains the Milosevic-Holbrooke Agreement, as well as the documents Mr. Vollebaek spoke about. These documents speak for themselves, but Mr. Vollebaek described them a little differently so I'll put some questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The standpoint of the Defence and of all of us from Serbia is that in Rambouillet the Serb delegation was led by Professor Ratko Markovic, who signed a political document, as it was called, and we agreed in principle to consider the nature and extent of an international presence for the implementation of any agreement that is reached. What the Serb delegation did not accept was a NATO military presence. Do you agree with this?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: I do not recall exactly what was agreed, what was said, because I -- as I said, I did not participate in the negotiations; but at that time, of course, I had access to the political agreement, as you said. And I suppose you are right, because the discussion I had with Mr. Milosevic was precisely on the international NATO-led military force. So I would think so. But I do not have access to those papers and, as I said, it happened eight years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: All right. Thank you very much. My next observation is the following. In Paris, when they met again, the Serb delegation did not go back from the political agreement that had already been signed, rather, the Serb, or rather, the Yugoslav delegation - we were still Yugoslavia then - did not want to sign the entire document in which, I repeat, NATO troops were to enter and there was to be a referendum on the independence of Kosovo three years later. That's what the Yugoslav delegation did not sign then, and let me tell you, no one in their right mind without sign it today. However, that's my comment, that's not a question.

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Again, I do not recall exactly what was agreed and what was not agreed to. My impression at that time, when I met again in Paris, was that there were a number of questions that had been accepted, that after the recess were taken up and discussed again, but this again is my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much. I think this had to be said. Now I will put the questions I have prepared for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes. It's not just a question of having to be said, though, Mr. Fila. If it's as simple as that, that there was introduced into the equation a term which would lead inevitably to a referendum within three years or after three years, then that's a very important consideration in trying to work out why these negotiations failed, because it's part of the Prosecution case here that the accused set about ensuring that they failed. Now, are you saying, Mr. Vollebaek, that you were not aware of a change in the terms as fundamental as that taking place between Rambouillet and Paris?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, again, this happened eight years ago, and I have to be careful. But as I recall, to be a little bit personal, I was in disagreement and I was quite upset at the time when those who led the negotiations allowed the recess, because I thought that was utterly wrong. I felt we had come quite far in the negotiations, and I knew there were difficulties. I'm not an expert but I have participated in some negotiations before this, and I knew these were contradicting any kind of experience I have. When you are close to an agreement, then you all of a sudden let the people off the hook and let them go home. But I -- as I said, I was just an observer and I couldn't really -- I didn't have a clout to say no. And when they came back then, it was my assessment - but it could of course be that I was upset and saw that they were -- and saw thought this would happen - that there were a number of issues that the Serb or the Yugoslav delegation came back and they had several points that they said they could not accept. It could be that this was under the overall impression of something that I felt strongly about, but there were a number of issues as I recall it that were discussed, not only one issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's even more fundamental than the way I've put it I think. I'll be corrected if I'm wrong, but I think the position of the Defence here generally is not only were they not intent upon making sure the negotiations failed, but it was the other way around. It was at least part of the international team that was intent upon making sure they failed by adding a clause that would be unacceptable.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And it's suggested that the Americans insisted on this referendum appearing as part of the fundamental terms, and thus they were intent on ensuring that NATO got in there to bomb Serbia. Now, you don't have this impression in your mind that that's what actually happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think you have to ask the Americans about that and not a poor Norwegian. But if I may, Your Honour, what I felt when the recess came was actually that the Serbs -- or the Yugoslav government had a kind of upper hand to a certain extent, and I thought that because the Kosovo Albanians were the difficult ones. And I couldn't understand why they wouldn't give us this, because they could actually have got quite a bit of praise from being more forthcoming than what they were. So my impression was that we had come quite far. And if I may, Your Honour, just to make it quite clear, at that time I was very much opposed to an independent Kosovo. So from my point of view, as chairman in office of the OSCE, I had absolutely no intent whatsoever of making -- making - what should I say? - taking steps that would lead to an independent Kosovo, out of a matter of principle but also out of a matter of my office as the chairman of the OSCE, where we had a number of -- and the OSCE still has a number of issues that deal with ethnic enclaves. And I felt that if Kosovo became independent, it would open up for Nagorno-Karabakh, Southern Ossetia. You have all these various areas under the mandate or where these issues are discussed within the OSCE. So I was very concerned with that from a personal point of view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: I have a question, Ambassador. I have a question. But you had in mind the suggestion that it should be like Aaland in Finland, like the case of the island of Oland. Did you have that suggestion? Did you propose that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not to my recollection, Your Honour. I know that some NGOs worked on this, and I know also that the -- whatever it's called, the local government in Aaland was very actively involved and trying to make that an example. To my recollection, I never mentioned Aaland as a case. What I was concerned with and what I told Mr. Milosevic on several occasions was that one had to find some kind of a -- I may have used the word "autonomy," at least some kind of way in which the Kosovo Albanians could have the rights to their language, to schools, to religion, some basic human rights. That was a great concern to me. But I also remember that we discussed the various ways that this could be organised, and as you will know there have been different constitutions for Yugoslavia. And under these different constitutions there were different status for Kosovo. And as far as I recall, I told Mr. Milosevic that I was not going in to discuss this. This was not my business and this could be done in various ways, as long as this was accepted and there were certain ways in there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two issues. First, in the political agreement that was signed, the rights to education and language were mentioned. And as for your question, Your Honour, about Aaland and the southern Tirol, that's precisely the package that the Serb delegation is offering to the Albanians now. We offered it then, too, but all they want is independence.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Sir, you took over leadership of the OSCE and the mission sometime in January 1999. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Yes, formally from the 1st of January, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And the presidency is one year, am I correct?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And then you said that the mission had finished its job, because on the 20th of March, 1999, you asked for the withdrawal of the monitors and that was four days before the air-strikes. There is a terminological difference because we consider it to be an aggression by NATO. Since there was no decision issued by the Security Council, you who participated in it. Call it differently, but we won't go into that now. What I'm interested in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Let's now concentrate on the questions, Mr. Fila. I think I've allowed you plenty of rope to make your comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you for allowing me to say what I said before. I won't say anymore.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: The question is the following: We have heard a number of witnesses, in particular Mr. Adan Merovci, for example at page 8524, who said that already in Paris Mr. Robin Cook and Mr. Huber Vedrine, who you said attended more of these talks than you did, told him that Serbia and Yugoslavia would be bombed within two or three days. Then they went to see Mr. Clark in Brussels, and Mr. Clark told them that they should get their women and children and themselves off the streets, because there would be air-strikes and NATO would be in Kosovo within a few days. Did you have any knowledge that after the failure to sign in Paris there would be air-strikes?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you allow me, I think I have to go back a little bit since this is a question that involves just more than a yes or no answer. First of all, when the Defence says that this was a NATO-led aggression, to me it was under a UN -- not a full mandate. I would have wanted a stronger mandate, but still there was an UN acceptance of using chapter 7 language. And for me this is a matter of principle, which is very important for me to make clear that I was under that understanding, otherwise I would not have accepted it. Secondly, I feel that it is implied in the Defence's question that I kind of opened the ground for bombing, which I reject very strongly, Your Honour. We had the KVM observers there under an agreement with --

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: We misunderstand one another. Allow me to interrupt you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, Mr. Fila, allow the witness to answer. I agree with you that he's probably read more into your question than he should have, but let him complete his answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe I recall, Your Honour, my presence here five years ago because then that was the -- I was charged with that. But anyway, I saw that the situation for the KVM observers were deteriorating, and they were -- there was aggression against them. So there were several attacks on them. And some of my colleagues, foreign ministers from other countries, threatened to withdraw their members because they said that it was politically impossible for them to have these people in the force. I told them that they shouldn't do that because that would, of course, put in jeopardy the whole mission, and it would show to Mr. Milosevic that there was a disagreement among the members of the group. And I said to them that as long as there are talks going on - and I told that also to Mr. Milosevic - as long as there are talks going on, I'm not going to withdraw. So please agree with me that as long as Mr. Milosevic, the Yugoslav government, accepts to be in the position of talking, we should have the troops or the forces -- neither the forces nor troops, but observers there. And the reason for this, of course, then was that I would not do anything that could put in danger the talks. So the moment the Rambouillet talks failed, my arguments were used. I had lost. So I had to accept that I had no reason to keep the KVM observers there any longer, since the talks were not going on. And we all -- I would say we all knew from press - you didn't need to do more than read the press - that there would be attacks -- a military attack on Kosovo after this. I did not know when, but I knew it would be coming. And as you will know from the transcript and my statement, I spoke to Mr. Milosevic on the 24th of March in order to avoid this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I have found it difficult so far in this case to establish when the decision was taken to attack Serbia, whether it was made before the talks took place and was thus conditional on the failure of the talks; or whether there was -- something happened after the talks to decide on bombing. Do you have the answer to that? Possibly not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have also found it difficult, and I think you have to ask someone else other than me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we have got closer to the horse's mouth, but I think failed to get the answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if you tell me when you get the answer, I would love to have it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Fila.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. Huber Vedrine would know the answer as Mr. Cook is not with us, and you know that he knew more about this. And do you know that Ambassador Mayorski also did not want to sign in Paris, the Russian representative?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: I think that is correct. I couldn't -- that is my impression, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Let's move on. Explaining your role in relation to the KVM, that's what we are going to discuss now, you said that you dealt mostly with the leadership of the mission while the leader of the mission on the terrain was Ambassador Walker. That's your statement.

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: And something that I would like to clarify is the following. What do you understand by issues of leadership and the structure of the mission? So that I can know what questions to put to you next.

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Your Honour, is it referred to at a paragraph that I could look at. I'm not certain that I understand the question. Is it the leadership in Belgrade or ...?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: No. I am referring to your leadership of the OSCE. You said that your involvement in the KVM was mainly about issues of leadership and the structure of the mission. I'm referring to the KVM, the mission, and it is not clear to me what the extent of your involvement was.

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you very much. Well, it -- as the OSCE is organised and as a consensus organisation, it has a secretary-general and a chairman in office, and the chairman in office is then a foreign minister from a country and it rotates every year. The political decisions for the OSCE would be taken -- or the day-to-day political decisions of the organisation would be taken by the chairman in office sometimes in consultations with two other ministers, the previous chairman and the coming chairman, so that they would form a troika. But under the OSCE, there was at that time and there still is as you probably know a number of field missions. The KVM was one of these missions and they have a leader, and the leader has of course the local authority. But he may be instructed by the chairman in office on at least major issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Now I understand. Then we could not ask you about the details, for example, the precise number of observers, the number of locations, and so on. Those would be details you would not be familiar with?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: At that time I should probably have known the number of observers, but I do not recall today. I think there were 300 and something at the maximum, but I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Sir, with all due respect, I don't want to strain your memory. Now I would like to know whether Ambassador Walker, as the chief on the ground, sent any written reports, either to the OSCE or to you as the chairman in office concerning the situation on the ground.

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Yes. There are rules of reporting. I don't know the frequency,, but there would be a number of reports sent to the OSCE on the -- on the situation on the ground. And I would have -- I don't think I read every single report. I, of course, could have had access to every one, but the secretariat in Vienna would have them all.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Yes. I understand. So the address we should apply to for Mr. Walker's reports would be the secretariat of the OSCE in Vienna?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: That is correct, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: You said that you contacted the Minister of Foreign Affairs Zivadin Jovanovic on more than one occasion. I have these reports. I will not show them to you because it was not you who compiled them but others. But would you please explain whether these meetings, one of which was attended by Nikola Sainovic, were constructive. How would you describe them?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: It may be difficult, Your Honours, to describe those meetings. But sometimes they were a little bit constructive, and I thought maybe that we moved ahead. But I felt very often that I -- it didn't lead any way, and at the end it kind of stopped. We had some specific cases that I managed to solve. We had a hostage case with some -- and we had the situation with the declaration or the threat of declaration of Ambassador Walker persona non grata that I managed to solve. So we solved some of the specific issues, but to describe them when I think back as very constructive meetings, I think I would have a problem with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. My next question is: How come you never saw the Milosevic-Holbrooke Agreement, that nobody showed it to you, and we have it in a book, in the book of documents from Rambouillet?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: That's a good question. I think at that time before -- at least before the Rambouillet, it was looked upon as something that was a bilateral or a kind of understanding. It wasn't an agreement that had been signed within the framework of the OSCE. It was Ambassador Holbrooke that kind of took an initiative, wanted to help out. And I don't know whether it was Holbrooke who didn't want it public or Mr. Milosevic who didn't want it public, but anyway it wasn't made available to me at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is this a suitable time to interrupt you, Mr. Fila?

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I have one more question and then it will be a suitable time.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: One more question I'm interested in is the following. You once said that you were at a KLA position. I would like to know whether you saw what kind of army this was. Did they have uniforms or not? What kind of weapons did they have? Light weapons? Heavy weapons? What were your impressions? And that will be my last question.

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: I don't think I could tell you I got an impression about the size or the structure of the army. I was taken to two posts; one from the Serb military post and one KLA post, in order to be shown how close they were, the situation in the region, the tension. And so that was -- and also, how the KVM worked with both sides. I think that was the structure or the reason for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. FILA
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Fila. We have to break now, Mr. Vollebaek, for half an hour. Would you please leave the courtroom with the usher. He'll show you where to wait.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Marcussen, I would still like these exhibit numbers for the various Rambouillet documents -- well, not the Rambouillet documents. The preceding documents mainly, the ones in October.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: We have some of them and there are some duplicates in our exhibits. So I would ask the Court's indulgence. We'll take the time to make sure we get the right numbers for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. We'll resume at ten to 1.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Sepenuk, is it you on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: MR. SEPENUK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We have no questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, just very briefly. Very, very briefly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, I want to refer you to that moment you were up near the border in Albania, and you talked to us about this matter of ribbons. Who did you go up there with? Who accompanied you up there to that location?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: I was accompanied by members of my staff of the -- of OSCE. It might have been someone from the Albanian government. I do not recall that, but it was from the OSCE staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And was it known by the people working up there at that location that you were going to be coming there that day?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: I don't know. I do not recall that. I recall that I was not very satisfied with the UNHCR presence and their way of being organised; so at least they hadn't -- if they knew in advance, they hadn't taken it seriously. But there were a number of other people who were very well-organised like local church groups and local NGOs that had been there already for some days.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I assume that a person of your stature arriving there and being there was -- kind of spread like wildfire. I think everything probably learned very quickly that Ambassador Vollebaek was present.

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: That could be. That could very well be. But as I said not everyone had done what they should have done if they knew it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Now, how far was it from the actual border crossing where you found yourself talking to people who had come across that border?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: It was on the border itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. And who had they encountered that you could see prior to your opportunity to actually have a chance to ask a question or something?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: I don't think they had had a chance to see anyone actually, because there was a long, long queue of people. And they -- I spoke -- I was standing literally on the border and I could, of course, watch them as they approached. And as I recall, they were not -- they didn't speak to anyone except among themselves probably, and then they were, as I said, met with an NGO as soon as they crossed and were given water and bread.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And the interpreter that you had with you that you used, where did that interpreter come from? How did you wind up with that particular interpreter?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: I always used OSCE interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So this was someone who worked for OSCE, that was an official OSCE Albanian interpreter?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: As I recall, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. And how were the people that you actually talked with, the people who you actually had a conversation with through this interpreter, how were these people chosen?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: I just went up to them and said hello or spoke to them as they passed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: No one chose them for me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, thank you. I hope I won't be much longer than my colleague Mr. Ackerman. As for my first question to the Ambassador I would like to rely on what Mr. Ackerman already asked about.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm only interested in asking you the following, Mr. Ambassador, can you recall and for the purposes of our Defence case what was the border post that you were at on that day that you discussed now with Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: No. I'm afraid not, but that of course we could find out. This was in the northern part of Albania. I visited two border posts; one in Macedonia and one in Albania. And I must admit I do not recall the name of the border posting, but it shouldn't be -- that of course are in the files and the archives. It shouldn't be very difficult to find.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, perhaps it's not much of a problem for me, but there is no interpretation, and I assume that the accused did not receive interpretation of the Ambassador's answer either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is there now interpretation?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now we can hear the interpretation, yes. But the answer was not interpreted at all, and I see that there has been a reaction on the part of the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Very well. Let's have the answer given again from page 85, line 3, of the transcript, in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, should I reply or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No, no. The interpreter will read what's on that into B/C/S I hope.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That has been clarified, has it?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, thank you. Now we have a full interpretation of the entire answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Ambassador, if I understood you correctly on that same day, you were at two different border crossings in Macedonia and Albania?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: No, that is not correct. I -- how should I say. During this process, I visited two border crossings; one in Macedonia and one in Albania, but not on the same day, two different occasions. I think, if I may add, that this -- there was only one border crossing into Albania. I think the refugees came only through one border post into Albania, so as I said it could be easily found, the name of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ambassador, today during the direct examination by Mr. Marcussen on page 44, the last two lines, 24 and 25, and 45, on the very -- at the very beginning, at the beginning of March when you were in Kosovo in the area of Podujevo, you noticed the presence of more troops than would be in accordance with your agreement. What agreement did you mean? It is unclear from the transcript.

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: There was an agreement, a signed agreement between, as far as I recall then again, the OSCE and the Government of Yugoslavia to the number of troops that could be posted to Kosovo. And one of the tasks of the KVM was to verify that this was not violated, that the number was according to the agreement with the OSCE. And we had heard or I had received reports from KVM that they thought that this number was increasing and that it could be in violation of the agreement, and this was also one of the issues that I raised with Mr. Milosevic when I spoke to him on the phone on the 24th of March, because I -- there was a lot of military people when I visited Kosovo in the beginning of March.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Mr. Vollebaek, can you remember the number envisaged by this agreement; that is to say, the force level?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: No, I do not recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: What would you say to me, Mr. Ambassador, if I were to put it to you that this agreement did not envisage a particular number of troops at all?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: I would say that I think you are wrong, but I do not have the agreement in front of me. But I was under the impression and I still am under the impression that there was a level agreed to.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Were you under that impression or do you know that for sure?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: As I have repeated several times, this happened eight years ago and a lot of things have happened in my life after that. And I must, in all honesty, say that I do not recall, but I was -- I do recall that I definitely was under the impression at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: I did not ask you about the number, but now you finally said to me that you were under that impression and that will do as far as I'm concerned. Thank you. I'll move on to my next question. Do you know that the representatives of the OSCE, with the members of the Army of Yugoslavia, at the time when Rambouillet was taking place - and we have heard testimony to that effect - assessed that there were less troops there to protect the state border from incursions by terrorists from Albania. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Excuse me, could I -- I don't think I understood the question. Could you repeat it, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Do you know that the representatives of the OSCE, with the members of the Army of Yugoslavia, assessed that there was a shortage of troops, especially to protect the state border, at the relevant time that we're discussing; that is to say, the Rambouillet negotiations?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Not that I recall, but there might be -- we may talk about two different things. One is the protection of the border and one is the presence inside Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And do you recall, since you say that there had been reports, how many troops were there in the field? Did your verifiers have actual figures as to the personnel levels there?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: That could very well be that they had and it may also be that that's in the report in Vienna. I do not have the figures here.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And if I say to you now, Mr. Ambassador, that OSCE representatives testified here and that in their testimony we can find assertions to the effect that they were not aware of such figures, what would you say to that?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: I would be surprised.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ambassador. Now I would just like to touch upon yet another topic. It has to do with the transcript page 45, lines 14 to 21. Again, it is the visit in the area of Podujevo in early March. It is not clear to me from the transcript. You said that you were born in the country and you know what the difference is between a haystack burning and a house being set on fire. It is my impression on the basis of this that you just saw smoke rather than what it was that was actually burning, right?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Yes. To my recollection, we saw smoke. But it was smoke coming out of clusters of houses, and we saw a lot of burnt-out houses and destroyed houses. So I was, as I recall it, very convinced at that time that one never talked about burning haystacks. And I told that to Mr. Milosevic in very uncertain terms. I was never in doubt at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: But, Mr. Ambassador, you didn't know whose houses they were, right?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: If you mean the owner, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And do you know from your reports. And we have here the testimony of a witness from the KVM. It was not a protected witness. I can even tell you who it was; it was Ciaglinski. The transcript page is 6902. I can read it out, actually, and I apologise in advance for my perhaps poor English. I'm going to read the question and the answer. [In English]" -- Also know as a result of KLA activities and the fact that they took control of large territories, another 36 villages were cleansed of Serbs and other non-Albanians while the mission was in Kosovo." [Interpretation] The answer of Mr. Ciaglinski is: [In English] "I believe that there was some of that type of cleansing going on by the KLA, yes." [Interpretation] And what was being referred to are 36 villages precisely in the area of Podujevo, where you were. Do you know of that kind of report?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Yes, I do. We had several reports also by KVM on activities by KLA or I don't know if we knew they were KLA, but by Kosovo Albanians that were in violation; and, of course, we addressed those in the same way as we addressed the other. I was told on this visit by KVM which knew, presumably, which villages were what kind, that these villages that I visited or saw having been destroyed were Kosovo Albanian villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And, again, as you said yourself, that is what you assume?

utterances.speaker: KNUT VOLLEBAEK
utterances.text: Yes. But it's a little bit more than an assumption, because we had, I would say, fairly good reports on where people lived and who did what to whom. And to repeat myself, we knew of very severe activities by the Kosovo Albanians that we objected to and protested, but on this occasion it was no doubt that this was done by Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have no further questions of this witness. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: And I would like to thank you, Mr. Ambassador, for your answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bakrac. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: No questions, Your Honour, for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I don't have any questions in re-direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That does complete your evidence to the Tribunal -- well, at least this Trial Chamber. I don't know if anyone else will call you back. Thank you for coming again for coming to the Tribunal to give your evidence, and you're now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: We now have to deal with the question of trial-related protective measures for the next witness, K79, and probably should do this in private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: That would probably be best. The filings have been filed confidentially and I think we should stick to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, we'll go into private session for that purpose.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I apologise. We had advised --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise. We had advised the Office of the Prosecutor that we would be moving to exclude the evidence of this next witness that is beyond the scope of the indictment. We could present oral arguments on that or if Your Honours wish we could probably get together a quick written submission on that and get it filed within the next two hours or so, so that Court could have it to consider. Just in terms of the fact that we do have some time. I don't know whether we could complete the discussions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What is the argument?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The fact that basically, Your Honour, there's two types of evidence that is contained at least in the witness statement for this witness. There is material from 1998 that is temporally outside the scope of the indictment; and then the material from 1999 that is listed, as far as we have been able to determine - we've cross-referenced all of them now - none of the events that are from 1999 relate to charged incidents in the indictment in terms of - and then they talk about crimes that are not even alleged. So, basically, it's the same arguments that were presented with respect to K83 whose testimony the Trial Chamber did exclude that what the Prosecution has done is take someone who is not relevant to this indictment and wants to present him with the aim of having the Trial Chamber make inferences from that about the alleged conduct that is relevant to the indictment, which we believe is -- would be an improper inference. The fact that this witness was not listed in the pre-trial brief as supporting this indictment and the fact that the indictment was not amended to include any of the allegations being made by this witness make it squarely a situation identical to that with K83, where we have a whole lot of evidence, none of which appears in any of the paragraphs of the indictment, specifically or generally. And we're concerned about that and we want to -- we want to -- we want to have that evidence removed. Now, at the end of the day, I don't know what would be left of this witness, if anything, but I think we need to have a clear ruling on that because, essentially, if it's not in the indictment, we ought not to be charged with rebutting it and defending against it because of the manner of which the indictment is supposed to serve as notice to the accused. So that's the just of our submission as I indicated. If you wanted details I could put them together in a written submission, but that's the gist of it and since we did have this time I wanted to bring it to Your Honour's attention now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What could you add in a written submission?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Just identifying specific paragraphs of the statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And then find what's not there?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And then find what's not there, right. I think, from our review, that there is nothing that would be left of the witness. I have not found a single one that was listed in the indictment, but I could at least categorise them at least from ones that are from the 1998 and ones that are subject to this objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Are you supported by this in any of your colleagues?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I have not had a chance to talk with any of them about it, so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I suppose one's as good as six in a situation like this, unless the others are anxious to retain the -- or to have the evidence of the witness. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, just with regard to your last comment, this witness is almost exclusively with regard to police activities and so most of us really have no interest in making that objection, frankly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But I would certainly support it if it's outside the indictment, as he says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Would you like me to address the issue of whether or not we should have written filings or would you like --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: No. We're not having written filings. We want to hear what you have to say on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, this witness is clearly relevant to the case, although my learned colleague is right. This is not a witness that testifies specifically about any of the charged incidents. It was mentioned that this witness is not referred to in the pre-trial brief; that's also correct. Now, the witness only gave his statement to the Office of the Prosecutor after the pre-trial brief was filed or just around the time when that brief was filed. So that's why there's no reference to the witness in the pre-trial brief. The witness was added to the witness list prior to trial. The statement has been disclosed to the Defence on the 31st of July. So I think it has been quite clear for a while that this is a witness that we find relevant, and it's unfortunate that we get the objection now that the witness is here. As to the relevancy of this witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: When should the objection have been made?

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: In my submission, when the witness was added to the Prosecution's witness list or before we -- we give notification of what witnesses we're going to bring a month in advance. We file a witness -- we file weekly notifications of what witnesses we're bringing. When these sort of things come up last minute, what it means is that we're bringing these witnesses up, some of which are sensitive witnesses in our view. They've now been exposed to the dangers that we think they're being exposed to by coming here and testifying. And it's just unfortunate that we get this kind of objection I think at this last stage. We are not -- we ourselves happen to be late at a time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I just wonder if there's another mechanism for dealing with this. I'm not sure that there is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Well, anyways, in terms of the relevancy of this evidence, one of the issues in this case is how -- how operations were conducted in Kosovo during the indictment period. As is clear from our pre-trial brief, it is the Prosecution's submission that there was a pattern established in 1998 in the way that so-called anti-terrorist operations were conducted in Kosovo. They involved excessive use of force. We have had evidence about how these operations were planned. What this witness brings is evidence from the ground about how these operations were carried out. The witness gives evidence about -- specifically about crimes committed in September of -- during a big operation in September of 1998. We've mentioned this operation in the pre-trial brief. The witness will give evidence about how the police and his unit in the PJP operated together with members of the army. The VJ, how they were attached to the company that this witness was in. They were assigned tanks and Pragas that regularly were used during the operations they went out on. So this 1998 evidence is critical to assessing the nature of these operations that were carried out in 1998 and, we submit, were carried out in a similar way in 1999. The witness also can give an overview of how the PJP was organised. He will mention the name of a number of people in his PJP unit. He will provide their radio call signs, which is relevant specifically to the assessment of which PJP units were involved in -- in the events in Suva Reka on the 26th of -- 25th and 26th of March, 1999, which is covered by the indictment. And the -- the specific evidence give about crimes committed in 1999, although it is not -- it doesn't relate directly to our crime sites. We submit that this is -- this evidence is relevant to assessing how these operations were carried out. The witness will say that he was given orders to expel Kosovar Albanians, for example, from their houses and tell them to leave the country. In our submission, this will clearly show a pattern of conduct and the evidence is, in our submission, very relevant for the issues that the Trial Chamber has to determine in this case, issues like the level of preparation that went into these operations. The witness is mentioning that before the operations that he was participating in in September 1998, his unit received orders from -- from officers that had been with Lukic in Pristina and how his superior officer would come back to the unit and launch these operations. All of this evidence is clearly relevant to this case and this witness should be allowed to testify. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, if what Mr. Marcussen has just told you is correct, we have a new and I think serious problem, and that's another failure of notice. None of the information we've been given indicates that this witness is going to have anything to say about any kind of joint operations with the VJ. And if somehow the Prosecution has that evidence, they've not given it to us. We don't have any notice of it, and the unfairness of that is patent on its face I think. Maybe he misspoke and maybe that's not what the witness is going to say, but if he is we certainly should have had that notice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Marcussen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MARCUSSEN
utterances.text: Your Honours, the evidence that the witness is going to give on this point the Defence have been given full notice of. First of all, the Defence have had the statement disclosed since the 31st of July last year. Secondly, it's true that the 65 ter summary was kept extremely short for the purpose of protecting the witness, but it's quite clear, for example, from paragraph 12 of the statement that the witness's unit was carrying out operations jointly with army units. So there's no surprise in that; and when we filed our witness notification last week, we specifically included a note saying that in order to avoid any misunderstandings, we wanted to make clear that we were going to lead evidence on every single point covered by the statement of the witness statement. So in my respectful submission there is no of notice issue arising from it in relation to this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. We will consider these submissions also and decide the matter this afternoon, if possible. That particular decision may have to await tomorrow morning, but if we can we will deal with it this afternoon and intimate the decision so that you're prepared for tomorrow whatever happens. We'll now adjourn now to 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 1st day of February, 2007, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.45 p.m.,
